idiom_name: stateless class, usually behind an interface, with constructor injection (Spring/CDI component when container services are needed)
implementation_notes: Model the operation as a class with final fields injected through the constructor and put its interface in the domain module, so callers depend on the abstraction; the classic role structure is replaced by nothing more elaborate than a POJO plus final references, because the JVM has no separate construct for it. Wiring is framework work - @Component/@Service scanning and @Transactional proxies from Spring, or plain new in a hand-written composition root - and a single-operation service can be expressed as a @FunctionalInterface so test doubles are just lambdas. Null-safety of the injected fields is the JDK's weak spot: keep them final and validate them in the constructor, or use Optional/Objects.requireNonNull.
pitfalls: A container-managed singleton bean is shared across threads: any mutable field - even a lazily-initialised cache - is a data race, so keep the class immutable and let the container choose the scope.
A @Service class that owns the transaction, maps DTOs and performs authorization is an application service in all but name; the domain class should carry only the business rule.
Injecting the container or reading dependencies from static holders (a service locator) puts infrastructure inside the domain type and makes the operation untestable outside the container.
